# Note 24 — The \(n=7\) Transported-Anchor Transition Groupoid

## every reduced two-spectator chart history is generated by three pair-local copies of the \(n=6\) wall operator

**Status:** theorem over \(\mathbb Q\), with exhaustive finite anchor census,
exact integer transition identities, and two-prime certificates

**Depends on:** Notes 20–23

**Claim boundary:** this note classifies every \(n=7\) coordinate obtained by
transporting a full-rank direct \(n=6\) edge anchor through an exterior
edge-response variable and completing it through the local matching
relations. It does not classify arbitrary quotient bases, construct a
transport map between different spacing words, produce a nontrivial closed
holonomy, or identify the exceptional quaternion with curvature.

---

## 0. Result in one line

Write the two spectators of a reduced \(n=7\) support as

\[
a<b
\tag{0.1}
\]

and fix the common core target in the ordered form

\[
T_7
=
\mathbb H_L\otimes\mathbb H_R\otimes V_a\otimes V_b,
\qquad
\dim T_7=144.
\tag{0.2}
\]

Let \(\theta:\mathbb H\otimes V\to\mathbb H\otimes V\) be the central
one-spectator transition of Note 20. If \(\phi_{\alpha,r}\) denotes the
operator which applies
\(\phi:\mathbb H\otimes V\to\mathbb H\otimes V\) to the factors
\(\mathbb H_\alpha,V_r\) and carries the other two factors unchanged, define

\[
\boxed{
A=(\theta^{-1})_{R,a},
\qquad
B=(\theta^{-1})_{R,b},
\qquad
S=(-\theta)_{L,b}.
}
\tag{0.3}
\]

Then every transition among the transported direct-anchor coordinates is
generated by \(A,B,S\). The three nontrivial generic words have the exact
chains

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
122:&\quad C_0\xrightarrow{\ S\ }C_1
              \xrightarrow{\ A\ }C_2,\\
131:&\quad C_0\xrightarrow{\ B\ }C_1
              \xrightarrow{\ S\ }C_2
              \xrightarrow{\ A\ }C_3,\\
221:&\quad C_0\xrightarrow{\ B\ }C_1
              \xrightarrow{\ S\ }C_2.
\end{aligned}}
\tag{0.4}
\]

The exterior words \(113\) and \(311\) have only one resulting coordinate:
all their admissible histories coincide.

For the exceptional word \(212\), there are two core coordinates, but the
intrinsic square residual is fixed:

\[
\boxed{
\begin{pmatrix}
C_1\\[1mm]\kappa_{212}
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
S&0\\
0&I_{\mathbb H}
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
C_0\\[1mm]\kappa_{212}
\end{pmatrix}.
}
\tag{0.5}
\]

Thus the first exact two-spectator groupoid is generated by copies of the
already known cross-product wall map. The exceptional quaternion survives
as a chart-independent summand; it does not shear into the core in this
comparison.

---

## 1. The finite class of transported histories

Let

\[
Q=\{q_1<q_2<q_3<q_4\}\subset G_7,
\qquad
G_7\setminus Q=\{a<b\}.
\tag{1.1}
\]

A **transported direct-anchor history** consists of the following data.

1. Delete either \(a\) or \(b\), leaving an \(n=6\) one-spectator support.
2. Choose any direct seed chart available for that parent support in
   Note 20.
3. Choose a parent edge block of full rank \(48\).
4. Require the deleted spectator to be leftmost or rightmost among the four
   variables retained by that edge response.
5. Carry the block by the corresponding exterior decoder of Note 22.
6. Complete the transported 144-row anchor through the \(n=7\) local
   matching relations.

For a generic word, the selected \(n=7\) edge must see the whole
144-dimensional quotient. For \(212\), it must see the whole
148-dimensional quotient so that the lift of every anchor row is unique.
This last condition excludes the two rank-144 outer edges of the exceptional
quotient: using either would leave an uncontrolled
\(\kappa_{212}\)-ambiguity.

The exhaustive census is

\[
\boxed{
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
\lambda&\text{raw histories}&\text{distinct core coordinates}
&\text{transition chain}\\ \hline
113&2&1&I\\
122&3&3&S,A\\
131&4&4&B,S,A\\
212&3&2&S\\
221&4&3&B,S\\
311&4&1&I.
\end{array}}
\tag{1.2}
\]

Thus twenty admissible histories produce fourteen core coordinates. The
collapses at \(113\) and \(311\) are exact equalities of integer matrices,
not only abstract quotient isomorphisms.

---

## 2. The inverse wall map

Recall from Note 20 that, for \(w,a\in V\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
\theta(1\otimes w)
&=
1\otimes w+\delta(w),\\
\theta(a\otimes w)
&=
-w\otimes a,
\end{aligned}
\qquad
\delta(w)=\sum_{\rho=1}^{3}
e_\rho\otimes(e_\rho\times w).
\tag{2.1}
\]

The polynomial identity

\[
\theta^{-1}=-\theta^2+\theta+I
\tag{2.2}
\]

gives the equally short formula

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\theta^{-1}(1\otimes w)
&=1\otimes w-\delta(w),\\
\theta^{-1}(a\otimes w)
&=-w\otimes a.
\end{aligned}}
\tag{2.3}
\]

Consequently (0.3) is a closed definition of three integral
\(SO(3)\)-equivariant automorphisms. No 144-dimensional fitted matrix is
needed to state them.

Their factor incidence is essential:

- \(A\) acts on \((\mathbb H_R,V_a)\);
- \(B\) acts on \((\mathbb H_R,V_b)\);
- \(S\) acts on \((\mathbb H_L,V_b)\).

Hence \(A\) and \(S\) act on disjoint factor pairs and commute:

\[
\boxed{AS=SA.}
\tag{2.4}
\]

The other two pairs overlap. Exact rational ranks give

\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{rank}[A,B]=64,
\qquad
\operatorname{rank}[S,B]=51.
}
\tag{2.5}
\]

The two-spectator transition system is therefore not an abelian
tensorization of the one-spectator wall.

---

## 3. How the three chains arise

For \(122\), deleting the earlier spectator first yields one right-parent
coordinate. Deleting the later spectator first yields left- and
right-parent coordinates. In the census order these satisfy

\[
C_1=SC_0,
\qquad
C_2=AC_1.
\tag{3.1}
\]

For \(221\), the mirror sequence is

\[
C_1=BC_0,
\qquad
C_2=SC_1.
\tag{3.2}
\]

The central word \(131\) contains both parent choices for both deletion
orders. It therefore realizes the full three-arrow chain:

\[
\boxed{
C_1=BC_0,
\qquad
C_2=SC_1,
\qquad
C_3=AC_2.
}
\tag{3.3}
\]

Every pairwise change of coordinate follows by composition. In particular,

\[
\boxed{
C_2=SBC_0,
\qquad
C_3=ASBC_0.
}
\tag{3.4}
\]

The same operators occur in different spacing words. They are determined by
which quaternion and spectator factors meet, not by fitting a separate
transition to each support.

---

## 4. Exact spectral fingerprints

All six operators below are integral and invertible. Their minimal
polynomials over \(\mathbb Q\) are

\[
\boxed{
\begin{array}{c|l}
\text{operator}&\text{minimal polynomial}\\ \hline
A,\ B&(t-1)^2(t+1)\\
S&(t-1)(t+1)^2\\
SB&(t-1)(t+1)^2(t^2-t+1)\\
AS&(t-1)^2(t+1)^3\\
ASB&(t-1)^2(t+1)^3(t^2+1)(t^2-t+1).
\end{array}}
\tag{4.1}
\]

The \(\Phi_6(t)=t^2-t+1\) factor first appears when the two operators
\(S,B\), which share \(V_b\), are composed. The full internal passage
\(ASB\) also contains \(\Phi_4(t)=t^2+1\). Thus the second spectator does
not merely increase the multiplicity of the original reflection-plus-shear:
overlapping pair actions generate new rotational spectral factors.

The repeated factors at \(t=\pm1\) show that these maps retain nontrivial
unipotent parts and generally have infinite order. The cyclotomic factors
alone should not be read as a finite-order holonomy.

The core target has a unique highest-spin summand \(V_4\). If \(P_4\) is
its Casimir projector, then

\[
\boxed{
P_4A=P_4B=-P_4,
\qquad
P_4S=P_4,
\qquad
P_4ASB=P_4.
}
\tag{4.2}
\]

So the complete three-arrow passage fixes the top-spin core sector even
though its lower-spin multiplicity spaces undergo the noncommuting
transition.

---

## 5. The exceptional word has no core–residual shear

For

\[
Q_{212}=(1,3,4,6),
\qquad
\{a,b\}=\{2,5\},
\tag{5.1}
\]

the maximal cross edge \((1,6)\) sees all 148 quotient directions. Deleting
\(a=2\) gives the spectator-4 right parent chart; deleting \(b=5\) gives
the spectator-2 left parent chart. Each transported anchor therefore has a
unique 144-row completion:

\[
C_0,C_1:E_{Q_{212}}\longrightarrow T_7.
\tag{5.2}
\]

A priori the two splittings of

\[
Y_{7,Q_{212}}\cong T_7\oplus\mathbb H
\tag{5.3}
\]

could have differed by a residual-to-core shear

\[
C_1=SC_0+\eta\kappa_{212},
\qquad
\eta:\mathbb H\longrightarrow T_7.
\tag{5.4}
\]

The exact computation gives

\[
\boxed{\eta=0.}
\tag{5.5}
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\boxed{
C_1=SC_0,
\qquad
\kappa_{212}\longmapsto\kappa_{212}.
}
\tag{5.6}
\]

This is a useful negative theorem. The exceptional quaternion is not an
artifact of choosing one of the two natural transported anchors, and it is
not already a path-nonconfluence term for this elementary comparison. It
survives as a chart-independent summand alongside the same generic
insertion-order transition \(S\).

---

## 6. What has and has not become geometric

Notes 20 and 24 now give a closed finite transport algebra:

\[
\theta
\quad\rightsquigarrow\quad
A,\ B,\ S
\quad\rightsquigarrow\quad
SB,\ AS,\ ASB.
\tag{6.1}
\]

The important gain is that the \(n=7\) transition matrices are no longer
uninterpreted \(144\times144\) outputs. They are forced pair-local
embeddings of the first \(n=6\) wall operator, and their noncommutativity is
controlled by overlap of factor supports.

This still is not curvature. Coordinate changes on one quotient satisfy
their groupoid composition identities by construction. In addition, the
first exceptional two-history comparison fixes \(\kappa_{212}\) rather than
producing it as a defect.

The next non-tautological target is therefore sharper:

1. construct elementary transports **between adjacent spacing words**, not
   only between coordinates on the same word;
2. compare two independently defined paths through that word graph;
3. test whether their difference lands in the intrinsic
   \(\kappa_{212}\)-sector;
4. if the first closed comparison is flat, pass to three internal
   spectators rather than renaming a coordinate transition as curvature.

**Subsequent resolution.** Note 25 constructs all six adjacent-word
transports from stationary shared edges. Their unique independent core loop
has exact identity holonomy. The exceptional \(\mathbb H\) vanishes on both
incident hinges and remains a vertex-supported defect rather than becoming
core curvature.

---
